# FFCy

FFCy is a *highly experimental* and at times *even more experimental* form
compiler for *the super experimental* [UFLx](https://github.com/FEniCS/uflx). It
compiles the action of a bilinear form, which is a linear form, on quadrilateral
and hexahedral cells to matrix-free kernels for NVIDIA GPUs and x86 CPUs. A kernel
computes the action on a batch of cells. It acts either on cell-local vectors
(E-vectors in libCEED parlance) or on a process-local assembled vector (an
L-vector) through a dofmap. Its output is MLIR (dialects `linalg`, `tensor`,
`arith`, `math` and `func`), which the bundled *custom* `mlir-opt` plugins and
standard MLIR passes eventually compile to an object file.

The repository also holds example forms in `forms/` and a benchmark harness in
`bench/`. It checks GPU kernels (NVIDIA CUDA, with or without scatter) and CPU
kernels (OpenMP, with the scatter in the driver) against a NumPy reference, and
reports their throughput.

## Prior art

I have read many papers on and attended presentations from authors of packages
like libCEED, Firedrake (TSFC, GEM, loopy, PyOP2) and FEniCS FFC(x). I have also
had many discussions with Chris Richardson on the structure of finite element
kernels on GPU hardware.

## LLM use

The pencilling and blocking transformations were almost entirely generated by
Claude Opus 5.5. The transformations were refined iteratively to their current
performant state by letting Claude Opus 5.5 iterate between MLIR/PTX and the
transform algorithms.

## How it works (TL;DR)

1. A front end written in Python converts UFLx/Basix forms into two xDSL-based
   dialects, `basix` and `uflx`. Laplace with Q1 elements on a quadrilateral, from
   `forms/laplace.py`:

   ```python
   gdim = 2
   degree = 1
   coordinates = coordinate_element(tp_lagrange(cell, 1, shape=(gdim,)))
   V = function_space(coordinates, tp_lagrange(cell, degree))
   v = TestFunction(V)
   u = Coefficient(V)
   form = inner(grad(u), grad(v)) * dx
   ```

   After pulling back to the reference cell, applying push-forwards and
   simplifying, the integrand is:

   ```
   Product(Abs(JacobianDeterminant),
           Inner(MatrixProduct(JacobianInverseTranspose(domain), ReferenceGrad(Coefficient)),
                 MatrixProduct(ReferenceGrad(TestFunction), JacobianInverseTranspose(domain))))
   ```

   In the `uflx` dialect this is:

   ```mlir
   #q1 = #basix.element<P, quadrilateral, 1, gll_warped>
   #gauss = #basix.quadrature<quadrilateral, 3, gauss_jacobi>

   func.func @action(%coordinate_dofs: tensor<?x4x2xf64>, %u: tensor<?x4xf64>) -> tensor<?x4xf64> {
     // Reference derivatives of u at the quadrature points
     %du0 = uflx.coefficient %u {element = #q1, quadrature = #gauss, derivative = array<i64: 1, 0>} : tensor<?x4xf64> -> tensor<?x2x2xf64>
     %du1 = uflx.coefficient %u {element = #q1, quadrature = #gauss, derivative = array<i64: 0, 1>} : tensor<?x4xf64> -> tensor<?x2x2xf64>
     // Jacobian components, and det J
     %j00 = uflx.jacobian %coordinate_dofs {element = #q1, quadrature = #gauss, component = array<i64: 0, 0>} : tensor<?x4x2xf64> -> tensor<?x2x2xf64>
     ...
     %det = arith.subf %a, %b : tensor<?x2x2xf64>
     %abs = math.absf %det : tensor<?x2x2xf64>
     ...
     // The flux paired with each reference derivative of v
     %f0 = arith.addf %c00du0, %c01du1 : tensor<?x2x2xf64>
     %f1 = arith.addf %c10du0, %c11du1 : tensor<?x2x2xf64>
     %y = uflx.integral %f0, %f1 {element = #q1, quadrature = #gauss, derivatives = [array<i64: 1, 0>, array<i64: 0, 1>]} : tensor<?x2x2xf64>, tensor<?x2x2xf64> -> tensor<?x4xf64>
     func.return %y : tensor<?x4xf64>
   }
   ```

1. `convert-uflx-to-linalg` lowers this to `linalg.generic` ops. Each evaluation
   and integration becomes one contraction per axis against a 1D table:

   ```mlir
   %table = arith.constant {ffcy.table} dense<...> : tensor<2x2xf64>  // 1D derivatives at the points
   %du = linalg.generic {
       indexing_maps = [affine_map<(c, i, j, r) -> (i, r)>,     // table
                        affine_map<(c, i, j, r) -> (c, r, j)>,  // u on each cell
                        affine_map<(c, i, j, r) -> (c, i, j)>], // result
       iterator_types = ["parallel", "parallel", "parallel", "reduction"]}
       ins(%table, %u : tensor<2x2xf64>, tensor<?x2x2xf64>) outs(%zero : tensor<?x2x2xf64>)
       attrs = {ffcy.pencil = 1 : i64} {
   ^bb0(%t: f64, %x: f64, %acc: f64):
     %p = arith.mulf %t, %x fastmath<contract> : f64
     %s = arith.addf %acc, %p fastmath<contract> : f64
     linalg.yield %s : f64
   } -> tensor<?x2x2xf64>
   ```

1. A set of 17 custom passes and standard upstream MLIR passes produce CPU and GPU
   code. In short:

   - **Sum factorisation.** The work is done one direction at a time (x, then y,
     then z), which keeps the cost low at high degree.
   - **Pencils.** Each 1D step works on lines of values through a cell, called
     pencils. These are small, independent pieces of work.
   - **Stages.** The action is grouped into a few stages: evaluate, apply the
     geometry, integrate. Pencils within a stage run independently, and each stage
     waits for the previous one to finish.
   - **Geometry.** It is either precomputed and read, or computed in the kernel,
     trading memory traffic for arithmetic.

   **GPU**

   - A thread block handles a few cells, with one thread per pencil.
   - Stages pass data through fast on-chip shared memory.
   - The kernel gathers `x` through the dofmap.
   - Results are scattered into the global vector with atomic adds, or through a
     separate summing kernel. Kernels on E-vectors need no scatter.

   **CPU**

   - Four cells share the 4 SIMD lanes of each core (AVX2), so the arithmetic is
     naturally vectorised.
   - A core carries one pencil at a time through a stage, keeping its values in
     registers and cache.
   - Each kernel is a plain serial loop over blocks of cells. Cores work on
     separate cells, as in DOLFINx's one MPI rank per core.
   - The kernel gathers `x` through the dofmap.
   - The caller does the scatter, such as the finite element solver, or the
     benchmark driver with a CSR scatter.

## Current limitations

- Only quadrilateral and hexahedral cells.
- Only Lagrange elements on GLL-warped points in Basix's tensor-product DOF
  ordering. This applies to the solution and to the coordinate element.
- Only cell integrals.
- Only scalar-valued function spaces.
- Only actions. The integrand must have exactly one test function and one
  coefficient, so FFCy cannot compile forms with several coefficients, residuals or
  assembled matrices.
- The quadrature degree is given to the compiler, not taken from the measure.
- Only double precision real values.
- Geometry of any degree is accepted. The tests and benchmarks only cover
  straight-sided cells.
- Code generation has only been tested on V100 GPUs (`sm_70`) and on AMD Zen 2
  CPUs (`znver2`).
- CPU kernels are blocked but serial. Parallelism across cores is left to the
  caller, for example through MPI.
- FFCy needs patched versions of LLVM, xDSL and UFLx, described below.
- No thought has yet gone into how to hook this up to DOLFINx.

A key question is how many of these limitations can be removed without special
casing everything, while still achieving excellent performance.

## Installation

### LLVM and MLIR

FFCy needs LLVM and MLIR 22.1.2, the version xDSL's CI tests against, with two
patches applied.

- `[mlir][linalg] Keep discardable attributes in elementwise fusion and reshape fusion`
- `[mlir][linalg] Vectorize insert_slice into non-trailing dims correctly`

Build it with the same compiler that will build the plugins, for example.

```sh
cmake -G Ninja -S llvm -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DLLVM_ENABLE_PROJECTS=mlir \
  -DLLVM_TARGETS_TO_BUILD="X86;NVPTX" \
  -DLLVM_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS=ON \
  -DLLVM_INSTALL_UTILS=ON \
  -DMLIR_ENABLE_CUDA_RUNNER=ON \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX=$HOME/llvm-mlir-22.1.2/install
cmake --build build --target install
```

`MLIR_ENABLE_CUDA_RUNNER` is only needed for GPU kernels and requires the CUDA
toolkit.

### Python

FFCy needs Python 3.11 or later, NumPy and pytest, and the following packages.

- Basix from `main`, built without UFL.
- [UFLx](https://github.com/FEniCS/uflx) and its `basix_uflx` package, with these
  changes, which are not yet upstream.
  - `conj` of a real-valued expression returns the expression.
  - `is_zero` and zero propagation through products, matrix products, inner
    products and sums.
  - Commutative operands sorted into a canonical order, so that real inner
    products commute.
- [xDSL](https://github.com/xdslproject/xdsl) with the attributes of `tensor.empty`
  printed and parsed.

`spack.yaml` describes a Spack environment with Basix, Python, NumPy and pytest.
It builds Basix from a local checkout, so first change the `develop` path in it or
remove the `develop` section. Then install the rest into a virtual environment
that can see the environment's view.

```sh
spack env activate .
spack install
python -m venv --system-site-packages .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e path/to/uflx -e path/to/uflx/external/basix_uflx -e path/to/xdsl
pip install -e ".[test]"
```

Run the tests with `python -m pytest`. Slow high-degree tests run with
`python -m pytest -m slow`. The tests of `ffcy.pipeline.run_mlir_opt` are skipped
unless `mlir-opt` is on the `PATH` or named by `XDSL_MLIR_OPT`.

### Benchmarks

The benchmarks for each target are a CMake project. Configure them from a shell
with the virtual environment active.

```sh
cmake -G Ninja -S bench/cpu -B build/cpu \
  -DMLIR_ROOT=$HOME/llvm-mlir-22.1.2/install \
  -DFFCY_PLUGIN_CXX_COMPILER=/usr/bin/c++ \
  -DFFCY_FORMS="mass;laplace" -DFFCY_DEGREES="2;4"
cmake --build build/cpu
python -m bench.sweep build/cpu
```

The GPU benchmarks are configured the same way from `bench/gpu`, and need `nvcc`.
Run `cmake -LH` on a build directory to list the other options, such as the
cells per block, the GPU chip and the CPU target.

## Performance (condensed)

Hexahedra (Q elements), double precision, throughput in GDoF/s, on one NVIDIA V100
and two AMD EPYC 7742 sockets (128 cores).

### Without gather/scatter (E-vectors)

| | Mass Q1 | Mass Q3 | Mass Q7 | Laplace Q1 | Laplace Q3 | Laplace Q7 | Helmholtz Q1 | Helmholtz Q3 | Helmholtz Q7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPU, precomputed | 33.1 | 31.5 | 32.7 | 11.6 | 11.2 | 10.9 | 10.3 | 9.1 | 9.1 |
| GPU, inline | 18.1 | 26.7 | 31.0 | 14.2 | 12.7 | 11.6 | 12.0 | 9.6 | 9.3 |
| CPU, precomputed | 8.5 | 8.4 | 8.6 | 3.7 | 3.8 | 3.6 | 3.4 | 3.4 | 3.1 |
| CPU, inline | 5.6 | 10.0 | 10.8 | 5.5 | 7.8 | 5.8 | 5.3 | 7.0 | 4.3 |

### With gather/scatter (L-vectors, GPU only)

Throughput counts global dofs.

| | Mass Q1 | Mass Q3 | Mass Q7 | Laplace Q1 | Laplace Q3 | Laplace Q7 | Helmholtz Q1 | Helmholtz Q3 | Helmholtz Q7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSR scatter, precomputed | 2.0 | 6.7 | 9.8 | 1.1 | 3.5 | 5.1 | 1.0 | 3.0 | 4.5 |
| CSR scatter, inline | 1.4 | 6.2 | 9.6 | 1.2 | 4.0 | 5.3 | 1.1 | 3.2 | 4.2 |
| Atomic scatter, precomputed | 4.5 | 9.3 | 11.8 | 1.4 | 4.0 | 5.5 | 1.3 | 3.4 | 4.6 |
| Atomic scatter, inline | 2.3 | 9.0 | 12.5 | 1.7 | 4.9 | 6.3 | 1.5 | 3.8 | 4.7 |

- **Precomputed geometry is memory-bound.** It reaches 80–100% of the measured
  bandwidth (798 GB/s on the GPU, 284 GB/s on the CPU), so it barely changes with
  degree.
- **Inline geometry is compute-bound from about degree 3.** It roughly doubles CPU
  throughput for Laplace and Helmholtz, but only roughly breaks even on the GPU.
- **The GPU is about 2.6–3.9× faster than the CPU** with precomputed geometry,
  roughly their bandwidth ratio.
- **Atomic scatter beats the CSR scatter** by up to 2.3×. With gather/scatter,
  throughput rises with degree because each global dof is shared by fewer cells.

See [benchmarks.md](benchmarks.md) for the machine, the setup and the full results.

## Size

The compiler is about 2,550 lines of code at commit `ccd28dc`. The count is
non-blank lines, without comments or Python docstrings.

| Language | Where | Lines |
|---|---|---|
| Python | `ffcy/`: front end, dialects, xDSL passes, pipeline | 1,409 |
| C++ | `mlir/`: the three `mlir-opt` plugins | 1,035 |
| MLIR (transform dialect) | `mlir/`: the three schedule files | 81 |
| CMake | `mlir/`: plugin builds | 22 |
| **Total** | | **2,547** |

Not counted:

- `bench/`, `test/` and `mlir/cpu/test/`, and the documentation.
- `ffcy/reference.py` and `ffcy/interpreter.py` (169 lines together). These are the
  NumPy reference and the xDSL interpreter wrapper, used only by the tests and the
  benchmark case generator.
- `forms/` (70 lines). These are the example mass, Laplace and Helmholtz forms, which
  are input to the compiler rather than part of it.

## Pipelines

The full order of each pipeline. Steps that are part of FFCy are in bold; everything
else is upstream MLIR. The schedules (`@__blocks`, `@__vectorize`, `@__bufferize`)
are transform-dialect sequences in `mlir/shared/blocks.mlir`,
`mlir/cpu/schedule.mlir` and `mlir/gpu/schedule.mlir`.

### CPU (`ffcy-cpu-pipeline`)

1. **`ffcy-fuse`**, which runs `resolve-shaped-type-result-dims`, `canonicalize`,
   `cse`, then **`ffcy-fuse-elementwise`**.
1. `transform-preload-library`, which loads the schedules.
1. **`@__blocks`**, run by `transform-interpreter`.
1. **`ffcy-sort-stages`**
1. **`ffcy-tile-stage-pencils`**
1. **`ffcy-slice-constant-indices`**
1. **`@__vectorize`**, run by `transform-interpreter`.
1. **`@__bufferize`**, run by `transform-interpreter`.
1. `scf-forall-to-for`, `canonicalize`, `cse`
1. `buffer-results-to-out-params`, `resolve-ranked-shaped-type-result-dims`,
   `canonicalize`
1. `buffer-loop-hoisting` and `promote-buffers-to-stack`, which allocate each
   block's workspace once, on the stack.
1. `convert-vector-to-scf`, `convert-linalg-to-loops`, `fold-memref-alias-ops`,
   `expand-strided-metadata`, `lower-affine`, `convert-scf-to-cf`
1. `convert-vector-to-llvm` (contractions become outer products),
   `convert-to-llvm`, `reconcile-unrealized-casts`

After `mlir-opt`, the build runs `mlir-translate` to LLVM IR, then `opt -O3` and
`llc -O3` for `znver2`.

### GPU (`ffcy-gpu-pipeline`)

1. **`ffcy-fuse`**, the same as on the CPU.
1. `transform-preload-library`, which loads the schedules.
1. **`@__blocks`**, run by `transform-interpreter`.
1. **`ffcy-sort-stages`**
1. **`ffcy-tile-stages`**
1. **`@__bufferize`**, run by `transform-interpreter`.
1. `canonicalize`, `cse`, `buffer-results-to-out-params`,
   `resolve-ranked-shaped-type-result-dims`, `canonicalize`
1. `gpu-map-parallel-loops` and `convert-parallel-loops-to-gpu`, which map the block
   loops onto a GPU grid, then `canonicalize`.
1. **`ffcy-atomic-scatter`**
1. **`ffcy-map-threads`**
1. **`ffcy-workgroup-allocations`**
1. `promote-buffers-to-stack`, `cse`, `canonicalize`
1. `gpu-kernel-outlining`, `canonicalize`
1. **`ffcy-check-mapped`**
1. `convert-linalg-to-loops`, `fold-memref-alias-ops`, `expand-strided-metadata`,
   `lower-affine`, `convert-scf-to-cf`
1. `gpu-lower-to-nvvm-pipeline` (to NVVM, then a fatbin for `sm_70`)

After `mlir-opt`, the build runs `mlir-translate` to LLVM IR, then `llc -O3` for the
host code.
